newsitem.title: USA: US court reinstates FCC rules for wireless firms.
newsitem.headline: US court reinstates FCC rules for wireless firms.

text.p: A U.S. appeals court in St. Louis said it has reinstated federal rules governing how wireless phone companies enter the local phone business.

The court ordered late Friday that the recent "stay" it imposed last month on key provisions of the Federal Communications Commisison's "interconnection" rules be lifted with regard to wireless companies.
The rules prescribe how long-distance carriers, cable-TV operators, wireless companies and other hook up to the local phone network under the provisions of the new telecommunications law.

Lawyers and analysts said the court's latest action represents a victory for wireless carriers. AirTouch Communications Inc., based in San Francisco, had asked the court to lift its stay of the wireless provisions.
"This is more than helpful for wireless companies," said attorney Alfred Mamlet of Steptoe & Johnson. "It's a win for them."
The court has left in place the broader stay of the FCC rules. But the suspension of the so-called "reciprocal compensation" provision governing wireless carriers has been lifted.
Under that provision, local phone companies must pay wireless carriers the same price for completing calls as they charge wireless providers to terminate calls.
Before the FCC's interconnection rules, wireless carriers did not receive any compensation but they did have to pay local phone companies for completing calls.

"We consider it extraordinarily good news," said Tim Ayers, spokesman for the Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association. "It really addresses the core issue of reciprocal compensation. And that is our central issue."
Lawyers said the appeals court's latest action does not influence its broader stay of the FCC rules.

But it does appear to add a new element into the upcoming case the court will hear in January over whether to overturn the rules, as requested by the Baby Bells, other local carriers and state phone regulators.

"This injects a new issue into the case -- the scope of the FCC's authority over wireless carriers under the telecommunications law," said Bradford Ramsay, a lawyer for the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, which is challenging the FCC rules in court.
